extracted.intended_audience: scholars, policy analysts, regulatory practitioners, and interest groups interested in how comments influence federal rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing which characteristics of interest group comments and commenters increase the likelihood that federal agency final rules will change to reflect those preferences. Focus is on formal notice-and-comment submissions to federal rulemakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment direction (support/oppose/modify)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment direction (support/oppose/modify) can shift final rule outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper identifies whether a comment supports, opposes, or seeks to modify a proposed rule as a meaningful dimension: directional stance is linked to measurable changes in final rule content. Use explicit labeling of stance when evaluating comment influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition / similarity of comments (volume/coordination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated similar comments from interest groups carry weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinated or multiple substantively similar submissions increase influence—assess the number and similarity of comments on the same issues rather than treating isolated submissions as equivalent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commenter expertise / organizational status
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsequent research has found that public organizations seem to weigh comments from expert organizations more highly than public comments in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between comments from expert/organized actors and general public submissions; attribute greater persuasive weight to organizational expertise, technical knowledge, or perceived credibility when predicting influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group type and kind of threat posed
rubrics_metrics.description: It matters what interests pose what kind of threat in regulatory rulemaking, with certain group types becoming more influential while others lose out when making specific kinds of threats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate interaction between the interest group's category (e.g., business, public interest, expert association) and the nature of their threat (e.g., legal challenge, political mobilization, information provision). Some groups gain influence depending on the type of threat they present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal participation (submitting comments)
rubrics_metrics.description: The formal participation of interest groups during rulemaking can, and often does, alter the content of policy within the 'fourth branch' of government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat formal submission itself as an enabling condition: whether a group takes the step to participate formally in notice-and-comment matters. Measure presence/absence of submissions and their procedural completeness as a baseline for potential influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome alignment: change in final rule toward commenter preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who voice their preferences during the notice and comment period rulemaking are often able to change government policy outputs to better match their preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use degree of movement in final rule text/policy outcomes toward the positions advocated in comments as a direct effectiveness metric. This is the primary dependent measure the study links to the other listed dimensions.
